This is the last book move of the Giuoco Piano: 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Bd2 (C54); both sides are on their own from here.

Nbxd2 is the strongest continuation, holding the balance at (+0.03, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nbxd2 d5 exd5 Nxd5 O-O], though in return White's pawn structure may grow weaker with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns deeper in the line—long-term targets that are often awkward to defend. Qxd2 was a comparable option, leading to equality on [pv:Qxd2 Nxe4 Qe2 d5 Bxd5], where a pin and a hanging black piece could emerge, but the recapture keeps the position level without inviting those sharp complications.

The most accurate response is 9...Nxd5, which holds the balance (+0.03, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nxd5 Qb3 Na5 Qa4+ Nc6], though in return White improves the pawn structure, clearing the doubled pawns and easing related isolated and backward pawn weaknesses. Ne7 also leads to equality on [pv:Ne7 Qa4+ Nd7 Qb3 O-O], a comparable alternative, but recapturing on d5 is stronger as White may soon coordinate knights toward increasing pressure on the black king.

The strongest continuation is 12.Ne4, which holds the balance (+0.16, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Ne4 Ne7 Neg5 Ned5 g3] and is set to put Black's king under increasing pressure deeper in the line—king pressure that often decides middlegame struggles. Rc1 leads to equality on [pv:Rc1 Nxd4 Ne4 Nfe6 Nxd4], a comparable option that immediately activates White's rooks on the open files and may improve the pawn structure in the line, yet Ne4 keeps the sharper initiative by steering toward that king-pressure plan.

per_ply.system_comment: Black passed up 20...Rd8, missing the chance to leave White with a hanging piece and to target the knight on d6; instead 20...Bd7 concedes a slight advantage to White (+0.03 → +0.60, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Bd7 Nh4 f5 Nhxf5 Bxf5], where White plays Nh4 and after...f5 pieces trade on f5 with...Bxf5 recapturing. 20...Rd8 leads to equality on [pv:Rd8 Qxc6 Bd7 Qc7 Qa4].

...Be8 targets the knight on d6 but concedes a clear advantage to White (+0.10 → +1.37, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Be8 Nhf5 Bf7 Rb7 Rxd6], and Nhf5 is the move that punishes it. The line may leave Black's king safer, yet risks White winning the exchange for a pawn. Black missed the chance to open the f-file for the rook with f5, which leads to equality on [pv:f5 Nxg6 hxg6 Rg5 Rf6], and missed the potential to leave White's pieces more passive.

The best move is 23.Nhf5, which maintains White's advantage (+1.39, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nhf5 Bf7 Rb7 Rxd6 Nxd6]. At the cost of sharper counterplay, Black's pieces are actively placed. By contrast, 23.Rxg7+ leads to equality on [pv:Rxg7+ Kxg7 Nxe8+ Rdxe8 Rxh7+]: it would immediately leave Black's pawn structure weaker and could eventually yield White a passed pawn on h3 in the line, but that path settles for a level game rather than the clear edge Nhf5 preserves.

Black's best option, 23...Bf7, still leads to a clear advantage for White (+1.27, Stockfish:16), yet [pv:Bf7 Rb7 Rxd6 Nxd6 Qe6] may eventually leave White with a hanging piece—a loose enemy is always worth chasing. Rf7 was clearly weaker, giving White a winning advantage on [pv:Rf7 Rxe8+ Rxe8 Nxe8 Qe6] despite the potential to target the knight on f5 in that line.

White missed the potential to win the exchange for a pawn and pin a black piece with Rb7, which leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Rb7 Rxd6 Nxd6 Qe6 Nxf7]. Instead, 24.d5 lets White's advantage shrink (+1.27 → +0.53, Stockfish:16) on [pv:d5 Rxd6 Nxd6 Bxd5 Rd7], as Black now has a bishop and two pawns for a rook while the continuation may leave Black's pieces passive. Rb7 leads to a clear advantage for White on [pv:Rb7 Rxd6 Nxd6 Qe6 Nxf7].

24...Nf4 makes matters worse, and White now has a decisive advantage (+0.53 → +4.34, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nf4 Rxa7 Nxh5 Rxa2 c5], as Rxa7 is the refutation. Black missed the chance to keep a bishop and two pawns for a rook—a workable material imbalance—and to leave the king safe with 24...Rxd6, which leads to a slight advantage for White on [pv:Rxd6 Nxd6 Bxd5 Rc7 Qa1+].

per_ply.system_comment: Black's 25...Rxf7 fights back, though White keeps a clear advantage (+3.29 → +1.40, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rxf7 Nh6+ gxh6 Rxf7 Kxf7]; in return, the line may leave Black with a hanging piece and could weaken the pawn structure with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns that are harder to defend over time. It still outplays Qa1+, which leaves White with a decisive advantage on [pv:Qa1+ Kh2 Rxf7 Rxf7 Kxf7], and grabbing on h5 next only deepens Black's troubles.

Taking on h5 with the knight makes matters worse, and White now has a decisive advantage (+1.49 → +4.54, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nxh5 Nh6+ Kh8 dxc6 Qd5]; Nh6+ is the move that punishes it. Black missed the chance to win a pawn and keep the king safe with Kxf7, which still leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Kxf7 Nh6+ gxh6 Qxh7+ Ke8]. With so few pieces left, this is an endgame now: king activity and pawns decide it. White remains firmly better going into it.

Nh6+ is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+4.27, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nh6+ Kh8 dxc6 Qe6 c7], with the line running through the king retreat, the c6 capture,...Qe6, and the c7 push that can drive the endgame forward. Rc7 also gives White a winning advantage but is clearly weaker on [pv:Rc7 Kf8 Qe4 Qxd5 Qe7+], making the rooks active on the open files right away yet only risking pressure against the rook on d8 deeper in that line.

Black gains nothing durable from this queen centralization, and the move makes matters worse—White now has a decisive advantage (+3.78 → +4.50, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Qd5 c7 Rc8 Rf8+ Rxf8], White answers with c7 and may steer the play toward Rf8+, the kind of forcing follow-up that tends to keep a winning grip in endings like this. Qe6 is a comparable option that also leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Qe6 c7 Rc8 Qf5 Qxf5].

The best move, maintaining White's advantage (+4.44, Stockfish:16) on [pv:c7 Rc8 Rf8+ Rxf8 c8=Q], advances the c-pawn and may lead through...Rc8 to Rf8+, the exchange on f8, and queening on c8—the clearest route to converting the edge. Rxa7 also gives White a winning advantage [pv:Rxa7 Nf4 f3 Qd1+ Qxd1] by winning a pawn and leaving Black with a weaker pawn structure, but c7 is clearly stronger by keeping the c-pawn as the main weapon instead of grabbing on a7.

Rf8+ is the strongest continuation in this endgame—the best way for White to maintain a clear advantage (+4.24, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Rf8+ Rxf8 c8=Q Qa8 Nf7+], at the cost of letting Black win the rook immediately. Even when Black captures on f8, White still obtains too much, as the line demonstrates. Qf5 is a comparable alternative that likewise leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Qf5].

Capturing on f8 gives White too much, and this move leaves White with a decisive advantage (+4.13, Stockfish:16). The main continuation [pv:Rxf8 c8=Q Qa8 Nf7+ Kg8] runs through immediate promotion on c8 and sustained pressure after...Kg8, with no offsetting benefit for Black. Even when White later plays the precise 31.c8=Q, that only trims the edge rather than overturning it.

31.c8=Q is the most accurate move, even though it lets White's advantage shrink (+3.72, Stockfish:16) along [pv:c8=Q Qa8 Nf7+ Kg8 Qxa8]. It immediately puts Black's king under pressure—often forcing awkward defense—keeps White's king safe, and gains space, at the cost of a pawn structure now weakened by doubled, isolated, and backward pawns. By contrast, 31.c8=R gives White a winning advantage [pv:c8=R g6 Rxf8+ Kg7 Rf7+] and wins a rook for a pawn, but may leave a piece hanging deeper in that line, which is why promotion to a queen is the cleaner choice; White went on to win.
